item.description:

Off-Meta Minute: Amber Amethyst Merida

Muuuuuum! It's just my bow!

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Nov 18, 2026

|

4 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Deck diversity has always been an appealing part of card games for me. As a competitor, I tend to prefer narrower metagames that are easier for me to target, but as a person? Let me turn up to my weekly event and play against every different flavor of nonsense out there. I wanna see what kind of brew gets you out of bed in the morning.

That's a big part of why I started Off-Meta Minute here on TCGplayer. If you cook up something cool, you deserve your flowers. Somehow, I have the platform to give them to you while also encouraging up-and-coming Illumineers to give your madness a shot. It's one of the coolest parts of my job.

Sometimes it's difficult to give the right person flowers, though. Sometimes, a sweet archetype pops up, and I cannot quite place where it originally came from as it lights up the tournament tables like wildfire.

That's what happened with Amber Amethyst Merida.

ELJ_GHartuck's Amber Amethyst Merida - 186th Place at Disney Lorcana Challenge Villain Challenge: Gaston 

I'd also like to mention Liam Dolecki's Top 256 performance with this archetype in DLC London's Main Event 1. The deck clearly has competitive legs; I just like GHartuck's list a little better.

This deck is a side grade to the more popular variants of Amber Amethyst with a few cute tricks baked in. We'll start with the namesake card, Merida - Wisp Conjurer.

 

We don't get Merlin - Rabbit or Genie - Wish Fulfilled anymore, but you can still accelerate into a pair of four-cost Amethyst characters that can draw you cards. You can lean on Mickey Mouse - Best in Town or Hamm - Piggy Bank within your first two turns to curve cleanly into a copy of Merlin - Profoundly Curious (who refunds you for the help) or a difficult-to-contest Merida - Wisp Conjurer that immediately draws a card and threatens to snowball out of control.

 

The best follow-up to Merida is often just a second copy, who can enter play exerted to draw you two cards in tandem with her counterpart. That's not enough to build a deck around though, so you'll need to rely on some other friends to help maximize the number of cards you can score from Merida. How do you do that? Bodyguard.

Rex - Protective Dinosaur is the best cheap bodyguard in this ink combination, regularly trading up for bigger characters and scoring you some lore in the process. Lionheart - Incumbent Mayor is an absolute tank with impossibly difficult stats to push through. Both will gain you incidental lore while banking cards of Merida, leading to an opponent who is frantically trying to bust through the wall to stop the card advantage while falling further and further behind.

But my favorite piece of spice? Remember Me. In those long, grindy games, it's not uncommon for an opponent to think they're running you out of cards before a Merida and a Hamm sing this backbreaking song, allowing you to play like three characters from your discard exerted and draw a card off every single one. You don't want to draw too many of these, so I like having only a single copy — but it's an army in a can all by itself.

 

I alluded to it briefly when talking about Rex and Lionheart, but this deck can close the door shockingly fast once those cards get spinning. Merlin's Shop and Smithy - Magical Market is an annoyingly sticky location that you can ferry your characters to for some extra lore and card draw. Even better, nobody wants to waste their time removing it. Once you enter the late game with a bucket of leftover ink drops, sometimes it'll just be sitting there waiting to win the game. It's a snazzy piece of cardboard.

I also wanted to mention how well the Demona - Imperious Spellcaster package slots into this deck. Of course, the namesake variant is a beast of a card by itself. It'll happily discard one of those cards you've drawn to turn into a turbocharged Madam Mim - Fox, but it can also fill the discard for a timely Remember Me in this shell. Demona - Betrayer of the Clan is also a phenomenal character to accelerate into with Hamm - Piggy Bank against aggressive decks and loves to be juiced up with Rush.

But the high roll? Use Demona - Scourge of the Wyvern Clan to lock down the opposing board before the Imperious Spellcaster sends her rushing into battle. I've had a handful of games where I've been able to play both of these cards with Remember Me and proceeded to blast my opponent's board to bits. It's very sweet.

Closing Thoughts 

I'm very glad that the Hyperia City metagame continues to offer some room to breathe for players who aren't enamored with Amber Emerald or Emerald Steel. Merida - Wisp Conjurer is an absurdly sweet card that didn't really get any time in the sun when it was released back in Attack of the Vine!, so I'm overjoyed to see players cooking up deck lists that allow her to shine. Is Remember Me the sauce? I don't know for sure, but I can't help but hope.

Have further questions? Let me know over at @HowlingMines on X (formerly Twitter) or @howlingmines.com over on Bluesky! Alternatively, give my other work here on TCGplayer a peek if you'd like another slice of everything nice about your favorite game. 

But until next time. I've been HowlingMines, you've been amazing! 

Stay safe out there — and happy gaming!

item.title: How to Upgrade Armory Deck: Dr. Mortimer
item.description:
Flesh and Blood|budget|competitive

How to Upgrade Armory Deck: Dr. Mortimer

Bloodrot on any budget.

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Nov 19, 2026

|

17 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

We've been scared of Dr. Mortimer for years now.

If you're a long-time Flesh and Blood fan, you may recognize the name from the flavor text of Arcane Rising's Back Alley Breakline or his haunting rendition on Compendium of Rathe's Lobotomy. If you're a lore nerd, you'll know him as the blight responsible for the horrific experiments carried out at Southmaw Asylum.

This is the man that fractured Arakni's psyche and left proud of what he'd achieved.

 

Dr. Mortimer knows exactly what makes the mortal machine tick...and what makes it stop. He honed his skills with both scalpel and study, diving deep into the writings of the L'Apocalypta cult about disease and infection. As infection bloomed through the pits, the good doctor stepped out of the asylum with the promise of cures for coin. It didn't matter much if he was infecting you with something else in the process. After all, inside the plague lies evolution.

Sometimes, you just want to play as the monster.

 

Armory Deck: Dr. Mortimer hit shelves at your local game store on November 13 alongside Mastery Pack: Assassin, introducing a brand-new way to enjoy the disruption heavy class. Dr. Mortimer, Blight of the Pits offers you the ability to fork opponents, outwitting them by sidestepping their expectations with a timely disease. All it takes to make the engine run is a little bit of currency.

Over the course of the game, you'll look to constantly inflict your opponent with a mixture of Frailty, Inertia and Bloodrot Pox. If the detrimental effect is beneficial? Great! Let it do some work. If it isn't? Use your hero ability to cure it for a Silver token, then cash in your Silver for a variety of powerful effects ranging from Go Again to additional damage. If the opponent thinks you're going big? Throw them off with your hero ability. Going wide? No no, here's a gigantic Expense Not Spared instead.

If been somewhat enamored with Dr. Mortimer, Blight of the Pits since I got this Armory Deck in hand. No two games feel the same, and so much of your deck is multimodal. If you find yourself feeling a similar way, let me have the pleasure of walking you though what you'll find inside the deckbox, some quick upgrades on any budget, and my full-powered machine that I'd register in a tournament tomorrow.

Let's get down with the sickness.

Armory Deck Dr. Mortimer - Full Preconstructed Decklist 

Armory Deck: Dr. Mortimer is a bit of a weird one to grade out of the box. The product exclusive cards? Strong. The reprints? Kind of stellar for an Armory Deck. Playability out of the box?

Eh. That one feels a little more disjointed.

 

There's some tension in trying to show a new player a little bit of everything that Dr. Mortimer, Blight of the Pits can do. Cards like Codex of Bloodrot and Pick Your Poison lean quite aggressive, but you're primarily a defensive pile of Frailty Traps, Inertia Traps and Viral Diffusions. You don't always need to avoid these non-bos in deckbuilding, but they do tend to cause confusion for newer players.

Escaped Subject's great, but you can't target it with Cut to the Chase or Act on Intel: Whereabouts. Those same six attack reactions cannot target Sneaking Rot, which is left relying on a sheepish mix of Seeker Kunai, Spreading Plague and Shred in order to activate at all. Again, there is merit in signposting everything that a hero can do inside of a pre-con, but when a hero's as flexible as Dr. Mortimer, it ends up feeling like a bit of a mishmash.

My best piece of advice is to lean into one aspect or the other as you begin your upgrades. You can become a more aggressive deck that leans into as many Codex of Frailty / Codex of Bloodrot / Codex of Inertia as possible alongside Escaped Subject, Scar for a Scar and other above-rate attack actions, or you can lean more defensive with enough power cards for strong pivot turns, going wide with Dr. Mortimer's ability when your opponent provides you the space.

Personally, I both prefer the latter and think it's the stronger archetype, so I'll be directing you that way in this guide.

Budget Upgrades 

You can do a healthy number of upgrades to the unhealthiest assassin without breaking the bank. To add some clarity, let me set some ground rules for cards that appear in this section:

  • At time of writing, no single copy of any of these cards will set you back more than $10 in its base rarity.
  • There is one exception to the above rule — finish out playsets that appear in part inside Armory Deck: Dr. Mortimer. 
  • I will not include tech cards or meta-specific cards in this section. While you may see some other cheap cards in the final full power list, they will be included due to their position in the current metagame. These are not the cards I would encourage you to spend a limited budget on, so they get skipped.

The Spider's Cut (Red) and The Spider's Cut (Blue) 

I'm shocked this one wasn't in the Armory Deck, frankly. I've been so impressed by this little all-star from Mastery Pack: Assassin for a few different reasons.

Firstly, it's absurdly efficient. One resource is the perfect cost for pairing with a dagger swing (or your Tunic resource in more expensive builds) and a disgusting rate for a six-power attack. The blue version still offers a breakpoint on a block-three. It's stellar.

 

Assassin heroes have so many pressing on-hit effects that your opponent does not want to be giving you equipment or defense reactions to deny Silver generation: it comes to you so easily anyway. The thing is? You will use every Silver you make each game.

You pay up front for the rate, but the on-hit that provides enough Silver for any of your other effects will force respect. That either allows your other attacks to find their mark later or leaves you rolling in it.

Remember the Mists 

If you're 100% on your enjoyment for Assassin but not entirely sold on Dr. Mortimer, Remember the Mists is going to be one of the safest investments you can make. This blue block-three stands to be a staple in the class for the rest of time.

 

The card really shines against opponents who intend to play arrows or plan to hold a defense reaction for their arsenal, but it's equally potent against those who wanted to play small hands. Wanted to keep Felling of the Crown and a blue? Would be an awful shame if I took that blue away from you, huh?

Remember the Mists will only get better if a mechanic like Inner Chi returns to Classic Constructed (as One Lotus appears to be teasing!) so I'd snap them up now. It's one of the best second-cycle cards you could ever ask for.

Expense Not Spared

These are riding the line on budget at the moment, but they're so good that I'd encourage you to skip a coffee to make up the difference if you need to. Most assassin attack reactions provide you with a timely +3 attack, making it the number that most opponents play around. That makes blasting them for +5 into a backbreaking piece of evasion.

 

It takes a little bit of practice to balance your Silver when an effect like this is lurking in your deck, but the yellow nature of it makes it perfect to pitch stack alongside an Excessive Bloodloss or similar.

Expense Not Spared's not how I want to feel about this card later. Grab your can of punch-em-in-the-face now and thank me later.

Patron's Lockbox: Valuables

As you may have noticed, Silver generation is the name of the game here. I think you need a couple of additional ways to make Silver woven into your resource base, and Patron's Lockbox: Valuables is currently my favorite.

 

When you don't need the extra currency, it's a blue block three. Otherwise, you're bound to complete a contract eventually (you've got bigger problems if you don't!). 

I'm a big fan of cards that allow you to convert your hand meaningfully when the opponent concedes tempo to you, and that's exactly what the lockbox allows you to do. Low floor, high ceiling kind of card in my books.

Codex of Bloodrot

This was my one price point exception because there are already two copies of Codex of Bloodrot (Yellow) inside the Armory Deck. It's really good, so I'm pretty sure you want three if you can.

 

Bloodrot + Ponder is a minimum of five value from the card even if you don't prefer converting to a Silver token or successfully disrupt the opponent's blocking preferences. While these are currently sitting at $15, I'm hoping the increase in supply from the Armory Deck helps to knock them down a peg in the near future.

Graven Walkers and Graven Cowl 

I'm not sure which of these you actually want yet, but they're a couple of cents each, so I'd just encourage you to pick up both and try them out. It's the best way to figure out which slot you prefer to give up.

 

While balancing Silver is a difficult skill to learn, I think a repeatable two-block piece of equipment is too strong to pass on. I've really been enjoying Graven Walkers alongside a Crown of Providence in the less budget-friendly lists, but I would probably lean on Graven Cowl if you're still rocking the Second Salvos.

Under the Trap-Door

Similar story here — there are two copies in the Armory Deck and you'd really like a third.

 

Pulling back additional copies of all of your traps allows you to punish opponents in reactions and create additional diseases/Silver. Watch out for spots where you can double-dip on Viral Diffusion and leave your opponent digging their fingernails into the table!

Spider's Bite / Nerve Scalpel / Scale Peeler / Arcane Lantern 

It breaks my heart to say it, but I don't think Humor Plunge is particularly good.

Assassins leverage their on-hit effects by afflicting your opponent with a detrimental block with your dagger before sending in your attack. That's achieved through a combination of Spider's Bite, Nerve Scalpel, and Scale Peeler in the weapon slot.

 

You'll pick whichever two are best suited for the matchup at the beginning of the game. If you're unsure, Spider's Bite and Scale Peeler tend to have some applications at least in most matchups. Nerve Scalpel really shines against Warriors and Wizards that don't typically play attacks, or decks that lean heavily on defense reactions.

Oh. Make sure you chuck an Arcane Lantern in there too. Don't want to randomly blow up to arcane damage against decks like Aurora, Legacy of Tempest or Viserai, the Forsaken!

Full Power Decklist 

Okay, so you've decided that you're in love with the good doctor. I get it; the deck is a blast. If budget is no concern, and you simply want to juice this monster to the highest level of tournament power, which cards should you be buying?

I'm glad you asked, mysterious voice on the internet.

If I was being forced to play Dr. Mortimer, Blight of the Pits in a tournament tomorrow, this would be the list I'd register for it. It's been incredibly fun, and I truly believe it has game into most of the top decks in the format.

Let's get into the nitty gritty.

Equipment:

Cadaver Handlers are broken. I said it before release and I'll say it again now. Card's messed up.

You make so many diseases, especially the proactive ones from your various Codices. It quickly becomes so difficult to profitably block your attacks, which is exactly what you want. While Cadaver Handlers are repeatable, most of the power comes in the threat of activation: your opponent can't block how they want to because you might use them.

 

The rest of your starting suite is fairly self-explanatory. Fyendal's Spring Tunic is wonderful in a deck with so many one-cost cards and often pairs with a blue to swing your dagger and a two-cost attack like Sick Intent. 1-card-6 off The Spider's Cut? Don't mind if I do. 

I've been liking the threat of Blacktek Whisperers too. Opponents don't enjoy denying it when you could always just tap Dr. Mortimer and spend some Silver to bail yourself out, and the extra extension can really help in those slower attrition-based matchups. That said, I could see you just rocking the Graven Walkers that we play into aggro in every matchup, or a Graven Cowl over Crown of Providence if you wanted space for something like Quickdodge Flexors.

 

Finally, you've got a copy of Mask of One Million Eyes. This exists solely to brick Hunter or Hunted? out of Arakni, Huntsman. Sadly, you need to do that to win the matchup, so you'll give up a single deck slot in order to make it happen.

Top Priorities

These are the cards I would prioritize picking up first if you're spreading the cost over a couple of months. It's not about the price here. We're not trying to grab a good deal; it's just about which cards I think are the most important to the hero.

Leave No Witnesses

There's a reason that the price tag on this one is climbing towards the moon. There was only a marvel rarity reprint in Mastery Pack: Assassin, which has left the hottest commodity in the Assassin class as the biggest must-have for new aspiring fans of the class.

 

Zero cost. Three block. Four attack that makes Silver and sends opposing arsenals into the abyss. This card really does do everything. It's also the single best target for Codex of Frailty, which leads us nicely onto...

Codex of Frailty

It was already the best card in Assassin and Ranger. What if it also made you a Silver and turned on Cadaver Handlers?

 

There is no card in the game capable of the same value and disruption as a Codex of Frailty. As sad as it makes me to say, you're at a significant disadvantage if you don't have them. Put them as high on your list as you can afford to.

Surgical Extraction

An annoyingly familiar story here. No reprint for Surgical Extraction in Mastery Pack: Assassin has this monolith trending back toward $25 per copy. It remains the most flexible blue for contract-focused assassin heroes and a staple you'll be glad to own.

 

Surgical Extraction is a large part of your endgame in matchups that come down to fatigue. Your biggest hurdle to victory against decks that continue pitching to weapons is removing those final four cards once the deck is empty. Remember the Mists and Surgical Extraction are perfectly designed to take care of that problem.

It's also just darn good against an opponent who wants to keep five cards.

Sick Intent

Sick Intent is a shiny new toy that stands out as best-in-class for two-cost red contract attacks. The contract clause doesn't much care how you create diseases, so while you'll usually just be looking to make some Silver from its own on hit, look out for spots where Outbreak can rock your opponent's world, or you can use your hero ability to send Wound Extraction as a second attack.

 

It's not uncommon to use a Codex of Frailty to pull this one back when you've spent two blues to swing your daggers, either. Wanna block this monster through Cadaver Handlers? Good luck!

Overcrowded

I'd actually like to find some space for more copies of Overcrowded in this deck. All of your diseases count towards its effect, so you'll find yourself with a cool five-block card if it lines up alongside Viral Diffusion.

 

The truth is that you'd really like to have this in your graveyard against opposing Codex of Frailty players, so you've gotta make space for a single copy at least. It's just a solid generic you'll get plenty of use out of alongside a variety of heroes.

Outbreak

It seems like most folks are lower on Outbreak than I am. That's great news for me because there's a chance that more of mine will get to land against an unsuspecting fool.

 

Sure, it ponders a little poorly. That's what Crown of Providence is for in a pinch. As I mentioned earlier, I love cards that I can both easily pitch stack and convert for immediate value if my opponent concedes full tempo to me. Outbreak might just be the best card in that department, so I don't think you'll see me with less than three.

Pain in the Backside

Another card that's become a bit of a mainstay for the Assassin class. Pain in the Backside is rarely a bad card, but it really shines against opponents who don't want to block. Additional ways to lock up a dagger on-hit certainly don't hurt.

 

The card is also a bit of an all-star against decks that demand you to go wide. If you need to slay allies from Gravy Bones, Shipwrecked Looter or Malice, Domina of the Dead, there's few better tools than a Pain in the Backside.

Plague Hive

The final pain point. Fabled cards are very expensive, especially when they're playable. Plague Hive has become one of those pricier bits of kit since both Dr. Mortimer and Outbreak were revealed.

 

I do think it's quite good in slower matchups though. A guaranteed Silver without needing to hit with the occasional upside of a backbreaking disease is one heck of a repeatable tool when the game goes long. It even provides you a safety net to make sure that you can play every The Spider's Cut in your deck regardless of your opponent's choices.

It's a boon, but it's probably the last priority to pick up from the priorities category.

Tech Choices 

I didn't want to leave you high and dry with no explanation for some of the remaining cards in the deck, so here's some brief notes about some of my tech choices that I don't think you have to play, but they're particularly nice against the current format.

There's a whole lotta blocking going on in the format right now. Nothing punishes a player who just sits back to block like additional copies of Shred. 

There's an argument for the red copies to really stick the screws into a Sink Below, but I like the yellow not only because they can be pitched to my daggers in a pinch, but I board in extra attack reactions into Ser Boltyn, Breaker of Dawn right now. The red ones would be pretty poor there, I think.

Unmake the Underling

Unmake the Underlings is your corner-case blue for punching problematic allies in the face. It's mostly here for Gravy Bones, Shipwrecked Looter, but you'll be glad to have it when you're staring down a Blasmophet, the Insatiable Hunger.

 

Don't be afraid to pull it back with a Codex if you need to. Just watch out for Fearless Confrontation!

Cutting Retort

I feel like I've been shoving three copies of Cutting Retort into every single deck I build right now. The card is so ridiculously strong against the top decks.

 

Between Runechants, Gate to I'Aratheal tokens, Flurry, Courage, Ponder, Fealty and so many more, everybody is pooping out tokens at the moment. The play pattern of pitching a blue to your dagger then spending a resource to suck up the problematic token and attack for five has been more impressive than praying my opponent doesn't block Violent Gusto, so Cutting Retort gets the nod from me.

Command and Conquer 

Finally, we've got to acknowledge the singleton Command and Conquer. This card is cheaper than ever (which is lovely) but I've slowly been decreasing my number of copies. It'd probably be the last card I bought for this deck.

 

The inability to use Cadaver Handlers, Shred, Cut to the Chase, Outbreak and Expense Not Spared on Command and Conquer really shaves points off its potency, That said, the various Dagger into Command and Conquer lines (including those with a Codex sprinkled in) seem a little too good to relinquish entirely. One feels like a good number right now, but I could see it going up or down.

Closing Thoughts

Woof. That was quite a wall of text. Thank you for reading!

Hopefully you've now got a better idea of what Dr.Mortimer, Blight of the Pits looks like from Armory Deck to full power in Classic Constructed. I've been having a blast wrapping my head around the deck and I'm excited to hear your stories as you begin plaguing your opponents with some disgusting diseases.

Have further questions? Let me know over at @HowlingMines on X (formerly Twitter) or @howlingmines.com over on Bluesky! Alternatively, give my other work here on TCGplayer a peek if you'd like another slice of everything nice about your favorite game. 

But until next time. I've been HowlingMines, you've been amazing! 

Stay safe out there — and happy gaming!

item.title: The Ultimate Black Friday Gift Guide for Pokémon TCG Fans in 2026
item.description:
Pokémon

The Ultimate Black Friday Gift Guide for Pokémon TCG Fans in 2026

When they say they want Pokémon cards, here's what they mean.

By Peter Day

|

Published Nov 20, 2026

|

6 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

The holidays are right around the corner! If you're hoping to surprise and delight a certain Pokémon Trainer in your life, you've come to the right place. We have traveled across the land (searching far and wide) to discover the perfect present for every type of Poké Fan.

Buying brand-new sealed Pokémon card products hasn't been easy in 2026. For the past two years, a boom in Pokémon card collecting has led to shortages of sealed product all over the world. While The Pokémon Company International has been reprinting waves of product to meet the demand, and card prices have come down as a result, many sealed products have remained stubbornly hard to find at MSRP.

It's not all doom and gloom, though! A few underrated gems are still totally affordable, and given how hard it's been to find great deals this year, your Pokémon Trainer will appreciate you putting in the legwork for them all the more.

These are the best holiday gifts for players and collectors of the Pokémon TCG in 2026.

Best Stocking Stuffer: Booster Pack

They like Pokémon cards? Get them a pack of Pokémon cards! Every Pokémon booster pack is basically a present already, with a delightfully rippable wrapper and unknown treasures inside.

The booster pack that Pokémon fans want to open this year the most is 30th Celebration, with Ascended Heroes as a close runner-up. Both of these sets contain huge hits that have dominated social media coverage in 2026.

Ascended Heroes has SIR Mega Gengar ex and "Treekachu," while 30th Celebration has the four-figure RGB Mew cards, plus 30th anniversary reprints of Lugia from Aquapolis and Base Set Charizard. 30th Celebration also boasts the best pull rates of any set in 2026, so the odds are higher that your recipient will pull something incredible.

Unfortunately, booster packs of 30th Celebration and Ascended Heroes are priced to match their hype. Plus, they aren't sold individually at retail (though you can get them on marketplaces like TCGplayer).

If either of those facts is a deal-breaker, we'd recommend Delta Reign instead. Not only is this the newest Pokémon set released so far (and the final set of 2026), but it's got the biggest hit of 2026 outside of 30th Celebration and Ascended Heroes: SIR Mega Rayquaza ex.

You can consider Perfect Order, Chaos Rising, and Pitch Black if you know your loved one is hunting a specific card from those sets. If not, Delta Reign will be the safest choice.

Best Gift Under $30: 30th Celebration Poster Collection

If this were a normal year, we'd be recommending the 30th Celebration Booster Bundle, which retails at an MSRP of $26.94. Unfortunately, in 2026 you aren't likely to find that product for less than $60 unless you get very lucky by visiting a major retailer right as it's restocking.

Instead, at this price point we'd recommend getting the 30th Celebration Poster Collection. This collection comes with three packs, any of which might contain an RGB Mew, plus three guaranteed promo cards of three Legendary Birds, and a poster with art from the set.

30th Celebration products have been elusive all year, and any Pokémon fan would jump at a chance to try their luck with the most tantalizing packs of 2026.

Best Gift for Collectors: 30th Celebration ETB

This year, the most sure-fire gift you can give a Pokémon TCG Collector without spending hundreds of dollars is a 30th Celebration Elite Trainer Box.

Elite Trainer Boxes (ETBs) are often considered the "default" Pokémon TCG product due to their price point and how fun they are to open. Each ETB comes with nine packs, a promo card, and loads of goodies. The boxes themselves are sturdy, and fans love them for card storage and display.

Many Pokémon TCG collectors try to get a Elite Trainer Box at every set release. Because 30th Celebration ETBs were so hard to find in person and expensive to buy online when they first came out, many fans had to put this dream on hold. Receiving it as a gift will feel like all those months spent longing are finally being rewarded.

There are arguably better Pokémon products near this price point. A Delta Reign Booster Box offers far more packs per dollar. The 30th Celebration Ditto Premium Collection comes with an acrylic card display that I personally prefer over any of the goodies in an ETB.

But the sheer quantity of stuff in an ETB, and its stature in the community, make it the most gift-y-feeling option.

Best Gift for New Players: Mega Lucario ex League Battle Deck

In previous years, it was easy to recommend that new Trainers pick up a copy of the most recent Pokémon TCG Battle Academy if they wanted to learn how to play the Pokémon TCG. Unfortunately, there hasn't been a new Battle Academy since 2024, and those boxes are way more expensive than a tutorial product should be.

For now, there are no Pokémon TCG products we can recommend to brand-new players. Instead, we'd recommend that new Trainers who can read on their own learn to play with the official Pokémon TCG Live app. It's 100% free (with no in-app purchases).

Once they know how to play, if your Trainer wants to face off against friends and strangers at a school club or game store, we recommend buying them a battle deck—specifically a League Battle Deck. These "Play Level 3" preconstructed decks come with a complete 60-card deck, and they're extremely powerful right out of the box.

The deck that won the 2023 Pokémon World Championships had 39 cards in common with the Mew VMAX League Battle Deck!

This year, the League Battle Deck we most recommend is built around Mega Lucario ex, a hard-hitting attacker with a few major tournament finishes to its name. Most of the cards inside (including Mega Lucario ex itself) will be legal through 2027.

The non-"League" battle decks like the Umbreon ex and Espeon ex Battle Deck don't offer near as much power, but if one of them features your Trainer's favorite Pokémon, it will still be fun to play. It's just not likely to win a tournament.

Best Gift for Experienced Players: TCGplayer Gift Card

Trainers who strive to be the very best need to update their decks with every new set, and sometimes even more often than that. A TCGplayer Gift Card will enable your champ-in-the-making to grab exactly the cards they need, when they need them. Plus, they'll always get the best deals on those cards, because they'll be shopping from hundreds of game stores across the country.

It's basically an UNO wild card, but for Pokémon (and every other trading card game).

Best Gift for the Trainer Who Has Everything

So you're shopping for a certified Poké Maniac. How can you knock their Wooloo fleece socks off them this year?

Every year around November, The Pokémon Company International releases a new Ultra-Premium Collection (UPC) designed to be the must-have gift of the season. This year, that UPC comes in two versions, based on the promos and the theme of the accessories inside.

Inside the Day or Night 30th Celebration Ultra-Premium Collection (UPC), Pokémon collectors will find a whopping 29 booster packs of the most exciting set of 2026. They'll also find two foil promo cards, a small mountain of goodies, and a bonus booster pack exclusive to these products with three cards from the 30th Celebration Classic Collection.

If money is no object and you just want to watch your favorite Trainer's jaw drop lower than it's ever dropped before, look no further. The 30th Celebration UPCs are the most coveted Pokémon TCG product you can buy in 2026.

Crush the Competition With Kazuma Kiryu from Yakuza: Like a Dragon

Crazy good synergies fuel the next big Cardfight!! Vanguard deck.

By Drew Knapp

|@FenrirRex
|

Published Nov 20, 2026

|

3 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

The wonderfully wild world of Yakuza is something that many (myself included) have poured hours of time into over the years. Yakuza: Like a Dragon in particular has become renowned for its twist on turn-based-RPG play mixed with a certain surreal sense of humor wrapped around a very unique plot.

Cardfight!! Vanguard saw a spectacular collaboration opportunity in Yakuza: Like a Dragon. Parallactic Dawn DZ-BT16: Parallactic Dawn has shown us all the fine results of that collaboration, and I want to sit down and talk about the killer Kazuma Kiryu core that has come out of the set for me.

A Wild Ride

Kazuma Kiryu does something distinct from most Cardfight!! Vanguard decks, in that you're playing your Grade 0, The Dragon of Dojima, Kazuma Kiryu, for the first few turns. He gradually tosses the rest of your ride line into your soul, gaining new abilities, before finally getting you easy access to your Grade 3. Meanwhile, your deck can be designed like a truly impressive toolkit, packed with cards that search for one another for a diverse array of interlocking synergies.

An Interconnected Crime Family

As you may have gathered by now, search effects are, in a word, good. Potentially starting with your ride line, the Yakuza build is designed to dig for specific characters that all love to see each other. In fact, this collaboration feels like it's trying to set a record for the number of cards that all mention each other by name.

Kaoru Sayama feels like a card you'd consider playing just for the bonus shield, but her power starts to really come through alongside Ryuji Goda, who in turn potentially further fuels your engine with Jin Goda. It can become surprisingly trivial to stack your bind zone and your soul to your advantage.

Yumi is the very definition of value when it comes to building up that advantage, joining up with Reina to form another block of synergy with Akira Nishikiyama. Akira in particular has already been instrumental in some of my best power turns, and I cannot stress enough how important it is for a well-constructed Yakuza deck to consistently access exactly those kinds of power turns. You can find yourself pushing for significantly more damage than your opponent if things swing your way.

Now, admittedly some of these synergistic kits want to consistently see each other on the board, and your opponent is unlikely to just be sitting there and letting you assemble every cog that fits into the well-oiled machine you're building. Yuya and Kazuki have stood out most to me as "work horse" cards, helping to keep you alive and drawing you into more value, respectively (and you need Kazuki for Yuya to play at its best!).

Everything I've highlighted has thus far played best as the core of the deck for me, but there is still some wiggle room for what else you want to run (and, indeed, in the precise number of even these core game pieces!). I'd be doing you a disservice if I didn't recommend Goro Majima as yet another card that makes your power turns even scarier.

But then, my core isn't necessarily something to be taken as gospel, it's simply what I've found has worked in my personal tinkering. You could, for example, start your build with a ride deck focused around Morning Glory: A Precious Place and Eldest Daughter of Morning Glory, Haruka Sawamura. That, in turn, lets you lean into Osamu Kashiwagi and Daigo Dojima for even more value.

So, what Yakuza brews are you building? Are you leaning into building all these miniature engines like me, or is there a more potent "goodstuff" build that you're succeeding with? I'd love to hear from you.

Top 10 Most Expensive Cards From Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek

O Captain! My Captain!

By Emma Merriam-Partlow

|

Published Nov 20, 2026

|

8 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek has been out for a little while now, and introduces an exciting way to fall into the game through the cult science fiction series. Admittedly Star Trek isn't for everyone, but there's some genuinely interesting cards if you can move past the red shirts and the Tribbles.

Star Trek cares more about collectability than any other Magic set released this year, and this is fairly common when you have a Universes Beyond property that has an avid fanbase that wants nothing more than to collect cards of popular characters and actors. That said, it's a little confusing to know what's valuable after cracking those Play and Collector Boosters, so I'm here to navigate you through it all.

Top 10 Most Expensive Cards From Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek

Today, I'll be going through the most expensive hits you can open from Star Trek. A fair warning that the cards discussed today only appear in Collector Boosters and not in Play Boosters, but expect prices to fluctuate as we swiftly roll into the new year. Since Star Trek is a franchise that cares deeply about specific characters and the actors that portray them, this currently dictates much of the set's secondary market value thus far.

#10 Will Riker, First in the Field (LCARS Showcase - Surge Foil)

Despite Star Trek missing the mark with many entrenched players, the set does boast some curious designs that haven't been done in Magic before until now. Take Will Riker, First in the Field as an example, who brings pseudo-ramp to the red color pie by putting two land cards into play at the beginning of your combat step. You do have to sacrifice those lands as you enter the beginning of your end step, but it's a really interesting way to introduce land ramp to a color that traditionally doesn't support it. At the time of publication, it's the LCARS showcase surge foil copy of Will Riker that's seeing the most value, as these appear in fairly low pull rates in Collector Boosters.

#9 Death Is Irrelevant (LCARS Showcase - Surge Foil)

The Borg make a huge-yet-lifeless impression in Star Trek, with Death Is Irrelevant being a notable card to support the artifact creature type. If you're someone who plays Necrons or Daleks in Commander, this is a card you'll want to consider for casual play. Death Is Irrelevant turns your artifact creatures into indestructible ones, with the upside to assimilate a creature card from any graveyard. This essentially means you yoink the best creature card going, turn it into a Borg artifact creature, and be on your merry way. Even though the eight mana cost is steep, it's one that can easily turn the tide of battle once you've had a turn cycle with it. That said, opening any copy of Death Is Irrelevant will bring decent trade value, but it's the LCARS showcase copy in surge foil that's seeing the highest value right now.

#8 Captain James T. Kirk (Classic Enterprise Showcase - Surge Foil)

This may be unsurprising if you're someone who follows the Star Trek franchise closely, but it turns out that many of the captains from the series are worth a pretty penny or two. Captain James T. Kirk is one of these, who's now seeing success in the competitive Magic space. Appearing in Standard Constructed's Boros Pixie (which also happened to be the breakout deck from the recent Magic World Championships), Captain James T. Kirk creates value upon entering or attacking. From creating Officers to boosting the power of your creatures, there's a ton of versatility that's already brought plenty of attention since Star Trek's release weekend.

There's already been price increases on all printings of Captain James T. Kirk due to the hype around Boros Pixie and how it's able to leverage other Star Trek cards in The Naked Time, so opening any copy of the captain of the Starship Enterprise will present you decent value. That said, it's showcase surge foil printing that's currently worth a good amount as it's exclusive to Collector Boosters, 

#7 Lieutenant Commander Data (LCARS Showcase - Surge Foil)

The same also applies to Lieutenant Commander Data, another surge foil mythic rare with extremely low pull rates in Collector Boosters. Data makes it so you'll put a +1/+1 counter on him whenever a player casts a noncreature spell, which means you can exchange those counters into pure card advantage. This card reads incredibly well, and one that serves best in a multiplayer setting where it won't take much for Data to dominate the game. One thing that's really interesting about Data's activated ability is that it doesn't specify just +1/+1 counters, meaning you can remove stun, -1/-1, or even keyword counters from a mixture of creatures you control to draw a card instead. This may not come up often, but it's one worth keeping in mind if you're looking to play with the card anytime soon.

#6 Captain Kathryn Janeway (LCARS Showcase - Surge Foil)

Being able to play additional lands on each of your turns is a strong bit of text in Magic these days, and Captain Kathryn Janeway offers this in spades. She's able to ramp you ahead on mana in a color that wants you to do it often, not to mention she rewards you for playing creatures as they'll explore upon entering as well. This is a pretty flavorful take on the Captain of the U.S.S. Voyager, giving you bonuses for exploring the battlefield with your own permanents. Despite generally being less popular than Captain Kirk or Picard, Janeway has her fans and there will be a subset of collectors who will want to own every treatment of her Magic card.

#5 Khan, Vengeful Heart (Classic Enterprise Showcase - Surge Foil)

A card that's seen plenty of discussion alongside Food Chain is Khan, Vengeful Heart, which sees the showcase surge foil printing becoming a desirable hit in Star Trek Collector Boosters. Other treatments of the card are much more affordable, but as Khan is a prominent antagonist in the Star Trek franchise, there's a desire to own the fanciest treatments for long-time fans of the science fiction series. Much like with Captain Kathryn Janeway, the flavor of Khan is on-point, since he's castable from exile and is able to create card advantage through sacrificing a creature or artifact you control. Being able to cast a creature from exile is pretty rare in design for Magic these days, so this is one that's worth picking up if you're after this specific effect. It doesn't come around often. 

#4 Mr. Spock, Science Officer (Classic Enterprise Showcase - Surge Foil)

Spock is one of Star Trek's most memorable and loved characters, so it isn't a surprise to see his mythic rare Magic card becoming an expensive hit from the release. Opening any version of Mr. Spock, Science Officer will present good value, with the highest multiplier coming from the showcase surge foil printing only in Collector Boosters. Spock comes with an exciting replacement effect that'll mean you'll draw two cards instead of one for each time you draw a card, allowing you to bury yourself in card advantage. This effect appearing on a four mana creature is quite the aggressive rate, and one that has a home in basically every blue-based Commander deck until the end of time.

#3 The Schematic Beam Me Up Promo Cards

Exclusive to the Beam Me Up Bundle are the stunning schematic cards, where you'll open two of eight random cards from this selection. At the time of publication, it's Deep Space 9 from this collection that's the most expensive, but opening any schematic card will present a modest amount of value. Deep Space 9 is seeing a lot of casual interest recently as it's able to throw permanent cards into play at the beginning of your upkeep from exile for free, meaning you can cast Spacecraft cards to your heart's content! This one can't be your commander, since Deep Space 9 doesn't come with any power or toughness.

After that, it's U.S.S. Enterprise-A, Free Spirit and Borg Cube seeing the most value. Secondary market prices around these Beam Me Up cards are a little skewed due to ongoing product delays with the Star Trek release, meaning circulation has yet to hit its peak. That said, these are some of the nicest and on-theme treatments Wizards of the Coast have done for a Universes Beyond release, meaning these will have plenty of interest from budding Star Trek fans.

#2 Captain Jean-Luc Picard (Showcase - Surge Foil)

A card you'll definitely want to pair alongside Deep Space 9 is Captain Jean-Luc Picard, who happens to be one of the best commanders to play from the Star Trek set. This card does quite a lot for three mana, from creating Officer tokens passive to searching up a Spacecraft card and putting it into play with a bunch of charge counters to boot. There's several reasons as to why there's interest in the various printings of Captain Jean-Luc Picard as of late, but I won't go into depth out of respect. 

#1 The Headliner Autographed Star Trek Cards

If you've been following the Star Trek release closely, it won't be a shock for you to see that the autographed cards are some of the most expensive ones to own from the set. There's seven of these to collect, and appear in Collector Boosters in extremely low numbers (approximately 250 copies per character in existence). Since autographed cards are very new to Magic, the secondary market value of these are a bit all over the place, but remain comfortably in the four-figure range to even five-figures depending on the signature.

item.title: All the Yu-Gi-Oh Lore in Magnificent Maestros, Explained
item.description:
Yu-Gi-Oh!|casual

All the Yu-Gi-Oh Lore in Magnificent Maestros, Explained

Rivals get a chance to shine in Yu-Gi-Oh's latest Magnificent set.

By Samuel Frew

|

Published Nov 21, 2026

|

18 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Kia ora koutou! Magnificent Maestros is upon us, bringing 18 more Grand Master Rares based on the cards used by major rivals in the Yu-Gi-Oh! anime and manga, a bunch of cards from the various anime for the first time, and several new cards from Toons, Witchcrafter and Unchained, all with varying degrees of lore and references behind their artwork, stats and effects.

Magnificent Maestros Lore Expalined

As with my article on the card lore in Magnificent Monsters, I'll be starting at the beginning. I've been looking forward to this article for a long time - let's get to the good stuff!

Kaiba's Cards

Kaiba's cards cover most of the arcs that he appeared in from the manga continuity (Duelist Kingdom, Battle City and The Dark Side of Dimensions), with certain cards being notably left out - look forward to their extended arts whenever we get Pride and Soul and the cards from the Original Artwork Collection!

Blue-Eyes White Dragon, the White Phantom Beast reimagines Blue-Eyes White Dragon, and much like Dark Magician, the Pharaoh's Servant, it takes inspiration from previous associated cards. Its name comes from the term used to describe it during the Dawn of the Duel arc in the Japanese version (in the dub, it's simply called "the White Dragon"). Much like the White Dragon, which Kisara called almost out of nowhere to defend herself, you can instantly summon Blue-Eyes White Dragon, the White Phantom Beast when you draw it or your opponent declares a direct attack. Its other effects reference other Blue-Eyes cards; the effect to destroy all your opponent's monsters is drawn from Burst Stream of Destruction, while the optional targeting immunity effect is similarly worded to that of Blue-Eyes Shining Dragon.

Deep-Eyes White Dragon, the Blue Abyss reimagines Kaiba's final monster from his duel with Yugi in The Dark Side of Dimensions, Deep-Eyes White Dragon. Its name also draws from Blue-Eyes Abyss Dragon, another reimagined Deep-Eyes (read as "Deep of Blue-Eyes" in the Japanese game, but using the kanji "Blue-Eyes Dragon of the Abyss"), which in turn drew from Deep-Eyes' summoning speech in the Japanese film, "Rise up from the azure abyss!" While the first effect of Deep-Eyes White Dragon, the Blue Abyss doesn't really relate to its appearance in the film, instead supporting the game-original Blue-Eyes support, its second effect is a roundabout way of mimicking Deep-Eyes White Dragon's original effect to Special Summon itself after a Dragon was destroyed and take on that monster's ATK (in The Dark Side of Dimensions, this was Blue-Eyes Chaos MAX Dragon).

Lastly, The Flute of Summoning Dragon becomes The Guiding Flute of Summoning Dragons, featuring Lord of D. in the art blowing that Flute with all his might to summon two Blue-Eyes White Dragons with one on the field, one of Kaiba's most famous moves. The first effect of The Guiding Flute working while the opponent controls at least two monsters harkens to Yugi's field at the time Kaiba played The Flute during their Battle City duel; Dark Magician and Beta the Magnet Warrior. Its second effect that allows you to draw a card references the manga, where Kaiba is inexplicably permitted to draw another card after The Flute of Summoning Dragon goes to his graveyard, and after he's finished attacking.

Zane's Cards

Zane Truesdale's cards are notably all based on his Season 1 Cyber Dragon deck - no Cyberdark stuff to be found here! 

Cyber End Dragon, the Final Strike Dragon reimagines Cyber End Dragon, Zane's most famous boss monster from Yu-Gi-Oh! GX. Its Japanese name is based on the Cyber Dragon Tactical-Try Deck: Decisive Strike. It inherits the piercing effect of the original Cyber End Dragon, and its effect to search Limiter Removal references one of Zane's more common combos to use with Cyber End Dragon. The triple attack effect is a reasonable addition to Cyber End Dragon, the Final Strike Dragon, given the three-headed Blue-Eyes Ultimate Dragon has been getting similar reimagined cards and Cyber Twin Dragon was a double attacker from the start.
Cyber Dragon, the Luminous Mech Dragon also takes its name from a Japanese Structure Deck, Structure Deck: Blitzkrieg of the Mechlight Dragons. While it obviously packs in the ability of the original Cyber Dragon to be Special Summoned while you control no monsters, it also seems to reference Infinite Impermanence (which features Cyber Dragon Infinity.

Future Fusion Nova reimagines Future Fusion, and its effect to instantly summon a Fusion Monster using Cyber Dragon in your deck while restricting your attacks that turn is reminiscent of its initial use in the anime, where it instantly summoned the Fusion Monster but prevented it from attacking the turn it was summoned, before being changed to match the real card. Naturally, Zane used this effect to Fusion Summon Cyber End Dragon, hence that monster appearing in the art of Future Fusion Nova.

Jack's Cards

Jack Atlas's cards have a notable omission, as there's no extended art reimagining of Red Dragon Archfiend, presumably because the designers didn't want to step on the toes of The Crimson King at the time.

First, there's a reimagined Crimson Dragon, Crimson Dragon Quetzalcoatl - in the Japanese version of Yu-Gi-Oh! 5D's, it's eventually revealed that the Crimson Dragon is Quetzalcoatl, during the episode where Jack acquires Blazing Soul and Red Nova Dragon (hence popping this monster in with Jack's cards). This version of the Crimson Dragon is DARK, like both Jack's monsters and the Ultimate God monsters from the 5D's manga based on the Crimson Dragon. The original five Signer Dragons appear in the art of Quetzalcoatl, Stardust Dragon, Red Dragon Archfiend, Black Rose Dragon, Ancient Fairy Dragon and Life Stream Dragon, based on a shot from CROSS GAME, the second ending theme in the Japanese version of 5D's, with its effects designed to recreate this appearance.

Regarding Red Nova Dragon, it's reimagined here as Red Nova Dragon - Burning Soul, named after Jack's Blazing Soul power (Burning Soul in the Japanese version) that he used to capture Earthbound Immortal Red Nova and create Red Nova Dragon. On top of sharing the original Red Nova Dragon's immunity to effect destruction, this monster's effects recapture its debut appearance, where it gained 2000 ATK from four Tuners in Jack's graveyard, and the effect of Burning Soul, a card used by Jack at the end of the manga referencing this power which could add a card from the graveyard to the hand.

Red Dragon Archfiend's Chains reimagines Fiendish Chain, which was debuted by Jack in 5D's. The art shows it binding three Shooting Star Dragons with blue, red and yellow hues; these three hues are the colors that Shooting Star Dragon splits into when attacking three times.

Kite's Cards

Kite Tenjo's cards cover both his ace monster from Yu-Gi-Oh! ZEXAL, Galaxy-Eyes Photon Dragon, and its original upgrade, Neo Galaxy-Eyes Photon Dragon, giving the latter some much-needed love after a lot of Kite's previous support hasn't really focused on it.

Neo Galaxy-Eyes Photon Dragon - Photon Howling is named after the initial effect of Neo Galaxy-Eyes Photon Dragon to negate the effects of all other cards on the field, hence the main effect of this card revolving around doing the same. Its artwork depicts it consuming one of its three Overlay Units (with the other two continuing to orbit it) before using its other effect to absorb all other Overlay Units on the field.

Galaxy-Eyes Photon Change Dragon is named after Kite's Photon Transformation (Photon Change in the Japanese version), which became the Photon Change card previously. Its summoning conditions evoke Hyper Galaxy, which could also Tribute monsters from both sides of the field with at least 2000 ATK to Special Summon Galaxy-Eyes Photon Dragon, while its main effect to replace itself with Galaxy-Eyes and temporarily banish an opponent's Extra Deck monster is a spin on the original Galaxy-Eyes being most effective against Xyz Monsters.

Galaxy Defense Robot Orbital 7 is Kite's robot sidekick, Orbital 7, which has previously appeared as both Orbital 7 and Photon Orbital. This time, Orbital 7 appears in his fighting mode, which he could switch to originally by removing his You Got It Boss! Counter and pump himself up to 2000 ATK, a stat that this monster has natively. Its name combines the Galaxy theme with Orbital 7's Super Defense Robot theme. As with previous Orbital 7 monsters, it focuses on card advantage for Kite's Photon and Galaxy monsters.

Yuri, Yugo and Yuto's Cards

For the cards from Yu-Gi-Oh! ARC-V, Konami eschewed doing cards for Declan Akaba and instead chose to complete the Four Heavenly Dragons reimagined cards after Odd-Eyes Pendulum Dragon, Four Heavenly Dragons in Magnificent Monsters.

First, there's Yuri's Starving Venom Fusion Dragon, reimagined as Starving Venom Fusion Dragon, Four Heavenly Dragons. This version of Starving Venom is also always a Predaplant monster, as Predaplants were Yuri's main theme, and its effect that activates when it's Summoned is a different take on the original Starving Venom's; while that gained the ATK of a monster and copied the effects of one, this Starving Venom reduces a monster's ATK to zero and negates its effects. As for its Super Polymerization-like effect, Yuri used Super Polymerization in the anime!

Yugo's Clear Wing Synchro Dragon becomes Clear Wing Synchro Dragon, Four Heavenly Dragons. As Yugo used a Speedroid deck in Yu-Gi-Oh! ARC-V, this version of Clear Wing is also always treated as a Speedroid. Its effect is a compressed version of the original Clear Wing, destroying a monster without waiting to negate its effects and gaining the ATK of the destroyed monster.

Lastly, Yuto's Dark Rebellion Xyz Dragon is reimagined as Dark Rebellion Xyz Dragon, Four Heavenly Dragons, although this version takes less cues from the original Dark Rebellion and more from Yuto's Phantom Knights deck. In addition to being treated as a The Phantom Knights card, it also has an effect to destroy an equal number of cards on both sides of the field, referencing Yuto's The Phantom Knights of Break Sword, which could destroy a card on each side of the field.

Varis's Cards

Varis had many powerful boss monsters in Yu-Gi-Oh! VRAINS, but Borreload Dragon was always the one given the most consistent importance, and it's this aspect of his deck that received focus in Magnificent Maestros.

His Borreload Dragon is now Borreload Liberator Dragon, accompanied by Rokket Tracer and Rokket Recharger in its artwork. Its first effect takes the Strange Trigger effect of Borreload Dragon and gives it the anti-responding properties of its Enemy Negation effect to weaken opposing monsters. Fortunately, it still has an effect to target your Rokket monsters, although this one works from the graveyard, akin to Borreload Riot Dragon.

Rokket Barrage features four of the original Rokket monsters in its artwork: Magnarokket Dragon, Autorokket Dragon, Anesthrokket Dragon and Shelrokket Dragon, hence its effect to summon up to four Rokket monsters. Triple Borrel Launch features Borrelsword Dragon in its artwork, and features three bulleted effects. Leaving aside the obvious bullet pun, it was Varis who would impart the three reasons philosophy to Playmaker during their youth to help him endure through the Lost Incident.

Anime Cards

Complimenting the anime cards from Magnificent Monsters, which covered unreleased cards from Yu-Gi-Oh!, Yu-Gi-Oh! 5D's (and Yu-Gi-Oh! 3D: Bonds Beyond Time) and Yu-Gi-Oh! ARC-V, Magnificent Maestros covers cards from Yu-Gi-Oh! GX, Yu-Gi-Oh! 5D's (again), Yu-Gi-Oh! ZEXAL, and Yu-Gi-Oh! VRAINS.

The three cards from Yu-Gi-Oh! GX are all from Season 2, tying into the currently airing remaster of Yu-Gi-Oh! GX in Japan. Demiurge Ema was the ultimate monster used by T-Bone, one of the Light Brigade who used the Monarch monsters and has had its effects vastly expanded based on cards that T-Bone used during his duel with Jaden Yuki. The effect of Shadow Moon that originally summoned Demiurge Ema is merged into this card, sending four monsters with 2400 ATK and 1000 DEF from the deck to the graveyard; in the anime, it was four Level 5 or higher monsters with different Attributes from the hand and field and T-Bone sacrificed Zaborg the Thunder Monarch, Mobius the Frost Monarch, Thestalos the Firestorm Monarch and Granmarg the Rock Monarch. Its effect to destroy a Spell or Trap and Special Summon two Homunculus Tokens draws from the Blue Moon Spell, which could turn two Spells or Traps into the Tokens. The 1600 ATK boost comes from the original effect of Ema in the anime, which gave it 800 ATK for each Homunculus Token in play, and T-Bone summoned two when he used it.

Sarina's Lord of Darkness (originally Dark Creator in Yu-Gi-Oh! GX) can be summoned by sacrificing Fairy and Fiend monsters, the main Types that Sarina used. It incorporates the effect of her Infinite Fiend Mirror to spawn as many Lord of Darkness Tokens as possible, including their balancing restriction that destroys them when it itself is destroyed and prevents them from attacking directly, while allowing them all to inflict 700 damage when they destroy a monster in battle.

Lightning Crash, despite its artwork and function, was not used by Thunder, the duelist who originally used Zaborg the Thunder Monarch, but by T-Bone, as the other Monarchs used by the Light Brigade had been added to his deck by Sarina, and the restriction didn't impede him, as he only searched Zaborg to sacrifice it for Demiurge Ema.

The Dark Tuner monsters are finally becoming a reality! Well, two of them are at least. Both Grady's Dark Tuner Catastrogue and Kalin Kessler's Dark Tuner Nightmare Hand inherit their exact effects from Yu-Gi-Oh! 5D's, but they bake in a unique method to Synchro Summon a Synchro Monster that recreates Dark Synchro Summoning from the anime. Rather than adding the Levels of the materials together, the Dark Synchro Summon subtracted the Dark Tuner's Level from a non-Tuner monster's Level to create a Dark Synchro Monster with a negative Level. All Dark Synchro Monsters are simply regular Synchros in the real game, so the effects of the real Dark Tuner monsters allow you sacrifice a lower-Level non-Tuner monster and itself to summon a Synchro with a Level equal to the difference, which works out the same for all of them (for example, using Level 10 Dark Tuner Nightmare Hand and Level 2 Infernity Dwarf created Level -8 One Hundred-Eyed Dragon in 5D's and the Level 8 Hundred Eyes Dragon in the real game).

Two iconic monsters from the Crash Town mini-arc from 5D's have also been released. Gatling Ogre is the most famous card from that arc bar none, as it was an OTK machine that Lawton famously drew every time he started a duel and was the first victim of Effect Veiler! It has a thrice-per turn limit on its effect; in the anime, Lawton only ever used or considered using its effect up to three times per turn. It also packs in the effect of his Back Attack Ambush Trap, which summoned Tokens equal to the number of opponent's Attack Position monsters that Lawton could instantly destroy to inflict damage and ended the Battle Phase; this effect simplifies this to inflicting damage for each opponent's Attack Position monster and ending the Battle Phase.

Infernity Doom Slinger was Kalin's counter to Gatling Ogre, and for the most part it's faithfully adapted, giving your opponent a choice to essentially play Russian Roulette or to cede any chance to inflict effect damage that turn. However, the penalty for failing the draw is simply a flat 4000 damage rather than the damage you would have taken; in the anime, 4000 damage was how much LP Kalin would have lost had Lawton called his bluff the first time he used Doom Slinger.

There are two cards from opposite ends of Yu-Gi-Oh! ZEXAL. Chaos End Ruler - Master of the Beginning and End was never used in a duel but was the ace card of a deck on exhibit in a museum that Scorch and Chills planned to steal, believing they'd be unstoppable with it. Considering that Chaos End Ruler was even stronger in the anime by virtue of also getting rid of the cards in your opponent's hand (being a combination of Black Luster Soldier - Envoy of the Beginning and Chaos Emperor Dragon - Envoy of the End) they probably weren't far off!

Hyper Rank-Up-Magic Ultimate Force was the final Rank-Up-Magic that Astral used in his duel with Yuma, Ranking-Up Number 39: Utopia Roots into Number 99: Utopic Dragon. It also gives a Number 99 monster it summons the enhanced negation effect of Utopic Dragon, with the Battle Phase limitation being because Utopic Dragon used this effect during the Battle Phase.

The final anime import in Magnificent Maestros is Bohman's Perfectron Hydradrive Dragon from Yu-Gi-Oh! VRAINS, his ultimate Link-5 monster from his last duel with Playmaker. While it had no Attribute-related effects in the anime, a rarity for Hydradrive Link Monsters, this card gains the LIGHT, FIRE, WATER and WIND Attributes in addition to its own EARTH Attribute and is unaffected by their activated effects; these were the Attributes of the five Ignis that Bohman had absorbed, with the Dark Ignis Ai the only one opposing him, and the DARK Firewall Dragon Darkfluid ultimately defeating this monster. In the anime, rather than having 5000 ATK, this card placed five Hydradrive counters on itself and gained 1000 ATK for each but could remove a counter to prevent its destruction; the real card simply reduces its ATK by 1000 instead.

Toon Cards

Pegasus's Toon deck was given a seven-card upgrade in the OCG's Revolution Booster: Toon/Witchcrafter/Unchained, and Magnificent Maestros brings these cards to the TCG, with monsters referencing ones that Pegasus used and effects that avoid Toon weaknesses and reference their use in the anime and manga.

Perfect Toon World is yet another Toon World reimagining, with art taken from the first activation of Toon World in the manga and a name drawn from Pegasus's claim that the Toons were the perfect life forms. Its effect to temporarily banish Toon monsters in response to resolution of cards and effects allows them to "dodge" them, as the Toons often did in the manga. The effect of Blue-Eyes Toon Ultimate Dragon provides this bonus to attacks instead, as the banishment occurs during damage calculation and doesn't trigger a replay.

Three of the new Toon support monsters retrain Pegasus's other monsters that were turned into Toons but haven't had Toon versions released and likewise become Toon monsters while Toon World is out. Dark Rabbit becomes Funny Dark Rabbit, named after Pegasus's favorite cartoon character Funny Bunny and taking on some of his aspects, like his goggles, colors and shovel. 

Animimicat is Mimicat (aka Doppelganger) as a monster, armed with Comic Hand and emerging from a book of his own, and his effect to sacrifice a monster and summon a Toon references the use of both cards in the anime to convert a monster into a Toon monster; Toon Summoned Skull against Yugi, and Toon Ancient Gear Golem against Dr. Crowler in Yu-Gi-Oh! GX. Lastly, Evil Box is Bickuribox, the winning Toon in Pegasus's duel with Kaiba, with the Level of the card in the manga, the color scheme of the one in the anime, and the non-Fusion status of it in both, and an effect to Special Summon its effect as Pegasus didn't need Tributes due to the Duelist Kingdom rules.

Dark-Eyes Illusionist Faceless Mage and Mind Scan are instead based on the more sinister parts of Pegasus's deck. Dark-Eyes Illusionist Faceless Mage combines Dark-Eyes Illusionist and Illusionist Faceless Mage and is an Illusion monster like both were in the manga. 

Mind Scan is based on the power of Pegasus's Millennium Eye to read the opponent's hand and mind and it's loaded with references. The cards in the art are Celtic Mystic, Griffoh, Chaos Magical Hats and Mind Shuffle, and when Pegasus read Yugi's hand at one point, he saw Celtic Guardian and Magical Hats in the exact positions their reimagined versions are in. Yugi also used Kuriboh during their duel, and the Mind Shuffle strategy to prevent Pegasus from reading his mind. The effect of Mind Scan to counter a card you name references Pegasus's talent for countering cards he knew were coming thanks to his own Mind Scan. The reason this card also works with Toon cards in your graveyard is that Pegasus continued to use Mind Scan after Yugi destroyed all his Toon cards. 

Witchcrafter Cards

Finally, there's the Witchcrafter cards. Their lore is largely centered around their leader, Witchcrafter Madame Verre, an important player in the larger Magistus lore.

Yu-Gi-Oh! CARD GAME THE CHRONICLES depicted Verre leaving the Witchcrafters to assist her former Magistus comrades, much to their dismay. Thankfully for them, Witchcrafter Celebration sees Verre return as Witchcrafter Madame Rilliona, with the age and appearance of her original self, Rilliona, the Magistus of Verre. The effect of Madame Rilliona and the art of Witchcrafter Distortion seem to imply the reversion may only be temporary and that she'll still return to the form of Verre without her impressive new hat.

Witchcrafter Potterie has become Witchcrafter Terracottan, and she's succeeded in making her little Stegosaurus even larger, but she's still having trouble with it! She also appears in the art of Witchcrafter Pupils alongside her fellow youngest apprentices Witchcrafter Schmietta and Witchcrafter Pittore, presenting a lovely colored stegosaur, likely a collaborative effort between the three of them given their magic specialities. Funnily enough, it's very evocative of Witchcrafter Unveiling, where Verre, Witchcrafter Haine and Witchcrafter Edel collaborated to create Witchcrafter Golem Aruru, and also of Witchcrafter Vice-Madame, which featured Haine, Edel and Witchcrafter Genni in its art (and which gets an extended art in this set).

Just like Magnificent Monsters, Magnificent Maestros was absolutely packed with lore and references celebrating Yu-Gi-Oh! and its past. Were there any cards from this set whose lore you particularly liked? Feel free to let me know on my socials!

The 10 Cards Everybody Wants from The Dominance of God (OP-18)

The saints are marching in.

By Joshua Calixto

|@HiThereJosh
|

Published Nov 18, 2026

3 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: The Cards Everybody Wants

The Dominance of God (OP-18) may not be an anniversary set or a heroines-themed special, but it packs in enough One Piece Card Game firsts to rack up similar levels of hype.

From Manga Robin, to a never-before-seen Straw Hat Leader, to a lineup of incredible alt-art cards, here are the cards everyone wants from The Dominance of God. 

#10 Mr. 0 and Ms.All Sunday Alt-Art

The early-series villains make their joint debut on this super-powerful alt. Not only does this card buff a blue Baroque Works Leader to 7000 power on the opponent's turn, it also draws 2 cards on play and can attach 2 rested DON!! to your Leader and Characters, meaning it can essentially refund its own cost when played. If it's not sought-after for its art, it will be for its sheer potency.

#9 Monster Chopper Alt-Art

Although this card is just a normal alt-art (albeit for a card that fits perfectly into the new Green Luffy deck), it's the first alt-art card we've seen of Chopper in his Monster Point form. Even if it doesn't fetch the highest sale prices, we expect this one to be popular with collectors.

#8 Mr.2.Bon.Kurei(Bentham) Treasure Rare

Region-exclusive Treasure Rares can be hit or miss depending on the character, but this one features Bon Kurei disguised as Nami. EB-01 did something similar with the classic Purple Bon Kurei SEC alt-art, so expect this card to draw the combined appeal of a Nami card and a Bon Kurei card.

#7 I'll Make the Call SP Event

One Piece's SP Events have always been some of its most visually striking, and this Gunko-centric SP is absolutely gorgeous, with a striking black background that comes to life in the light as the textures show their full elegance.

#6 Loki Alt-Art by Yoshitaka Amano

OP-17 had guest art from Baki the Grappler artist Keisuke Itagaki, and OP-18 brings two guest entries from legendary Final Fantasy character artist Yoshitaka Amano.

Amano's first guest piece is a reprint of the Loki SEC from OP-17, and it also comes in a fancy Gold Parallel version.

#5 Saint Shamrock Alt-Art by Yoshitaka Amano

This Saint Shamrock alt-art isn't an SP like Loki, but it does come in a rarer version modeled on the "demon pack" Five Elders from OP-13, with a special metallic border and a pentagram around the card's cost.

#4 Franky Alt-Art Leader

The suuuuuuper long-awaited Franky Leader makes his first appearance in OP-18, and three years' worth of unsatisfied fans will finally get their chance to collect his alt-art Leader. Rendered in the set's mural-esque alt-art Leader style, this may not be one of the rarer hits in The Dominance of God, but it'll certainly be one of the most popular.

#3 Saint Gunko Holy Knights of God Super Alt-Art

Like the Pirate Crew alt-arts that were introduced in OP-17, this detailed Gunko Character card features the Holy Knights of God in the background, rendered in a similar style. The original Pirate Crew alts were some of the most sought-after cards in The World's Strongest Warriors, and we expect this one to be just as popular. 

#2 Saint Gunko Super Alt-Art (Manga) Leader

Super Alt-Art Leader cards premiered in OP-17 with Elbaph Luffy, and have proven to be some of the most sought-after chases ever since, with EB-05 Robin fetching similar levels of attention. The Dominance of God (OP-18) sees the debut of Saint Gunko, a fan-favorite antagonist from the Elbaph arc, and her Super Alt-Art card is poised to be one of the biggest chases of the set.

#1 Manga Nico Robin

Nico Robin has always been a One Piece fan-favorite character, and OP-18 gives her her first-ever Manga Rare. Considering the last few sets featured Shirahoshi and the original Four Emperors as their Mangas (which are popular, but not Robin popular), Robin is slated to be one of the most hyped Manga Rares the One Piece Card Game has ever seen.
